title: Karma of the yogi — neither white nor black (4.7)
hook: most people's actions come in three colors; Patanjali says the yogi's come in none

segments.voice: Yesterday: kshetrika, the farmer. Practice doesn't push the water; it opens the wall, and nature flows.

Laundry day. Three piles on the bedroom floor: the whites, the darks, and the mixed heap that's a bit of both. Everything goes somewhere. Patanjali sorts human action the same way, by color, and he names the piles. Then, in one short line of the fourth chapter, he says the action of someone who has gone all the way in yoga goes in no pile at all.
screen: `THREE PILES ON THE FLOOR.` → `ACTION, SORTED BY COLOR.` → `AND ONE KIND IN NO PILE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.7: karma ashukla-akrishnam yoginas, trividham itaresham. The action of the yogi is not white and not black. For everyone else, it is of three kinds. Shukla means white, or bright. Krishna here means black, or dark. The old commentary attributed to Vyasa spells out the three. Black is action that harms. Mixed, black-and-white, is ordinary action: it does good, but it leans on outward means and touches others, so it's never perfectly clean. White is action done inwardly, through discipline, study and meditation. All three leave seeds, bright or dark, and seeds sprout. That's the surprise: for Patanjali, white karma isn't the finish line. A gold chain still holds you. So what is the fourth kind, neither white nor black? The commentators describe someone whose afflictions have worn thin, who acts without craving the fruit. The act still happens. Food gets cooked, the sick get visited. But nothing new is sown, because nobody is standing there waiting for the harvest. It's close to what Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. So the line isn't saying the yogi stops caring about good and harm. The yogi's good is done without a hand held out.
screen: `WHITE, BLACK, AND MIXED.` · `ALL THREE LEAVE SEEDS.` · `A GOLD CHAIN STILL HOLDS YOU.` · `NEITHER: ACTION WITHOUT THE HAND OUT.` · then, large: `KARMĀŚUKLĀKṚṢṆAṂ YOGINAS TRIVIDHAM ITAREṢĀM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one kind thing you did recently, and notice if anything is stuck to it: a wish to be thanked, to be seen as good, to have it count. See that wish the way you'd see a sticker on a piece of fruit, and peel it off. The act stands by itself; it happened, and it was good.
Ashukla-akrishna, neither white nor black. The yogi's karma, done fully and left free of its fruit, so it plants no seed.
Your line: neither. Not white, not black, and no new seed left behind. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often read 4.7 alongside the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on action without attachment to its fruit, and some practitioners try to do service quietly, without seeking credit.

fork.setup: Patanjali sorts action by color. which kind does he give to the yogi?
fork.reveal: neither. even bright karma leaves seeds; the yogi's action, done without craving its fruit, leaves none.

original.note: Sanskrit: a (not) + shukla (white) + a (not) + krishna (black). neither white nor black.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga is about piling up good karma.
what it means: good and bad karma both leave seeds; the yogi's action, free of craving, is neither.

what a scholar hears: the commentary on 4.7 names four classes, black, black-white, white, and neither; the first three ripen, and the next sutra says only the impressions fit for their ripening come forward.
recall: one-pointed: a mind on a single object
guess: action neither white nor black: done free of its fruit
purely good karma that earns the brightest rewards
mixed action, partly helpful and partly harmful

chat.says: Isn't doing good things enough? Why would good karma still be a problem for a yogi?
options: Even good deeds done for a reward leave seeds. The yogi acts without wanting the fruit.
Patanjali tells the yogi to stop doing good things altogether, to be safe.
Patanjali calls white karma the finish line, so just keep piling it up.
chat.meaning: In sutra 4.7, white, black and mixed karma all leave seeds. The yogi's action is neither, done without craving its fruit.

Vyasa.meaning: the sage to whom the oldest commentary is attributed

Arjuna.meaning: the warrior prince Krishna teaches in the Bhagavad Gita

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 4.7, Vyasa's commentary (the four classes of karma)
Bhagavad Gita 2.47 (your right is to the work, not its fruits)

notes: The four classes (black, black-white, white, neither) follow the Vyasa commentary as commonly summarized; confirm the description of 'white' as action through austerity, study and meditation, done inwardly.
'A gold chain still holds you' is the script's own image, not a quotation.
